summary:
Namibia's Supreme Court ruled on 16 May 2023 that same-sex marriages performed abroad must be recognised under the Immigration Act, granting non-Namibian spouses the same residence rights as opposite-sex spouses. Compliance has failed: immigration officials tell litigant Daniel Digashu that the ruling covers only the couples who brought the case, and he is issued a visitor's visa on every exit. Gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than to "all persons".

Parliament answered the litigation with hostile marriage bills and, in late 2024, passed an act explicitly forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad, overriding the Supreme Court ruling. Reporting that amplified the non-implementation compounded the effect, according to an op-ed by Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre published by the Washington Blade on 22 May 2024.

On 21 June 2024 the High Court of Windhoek declared unconstitutional and invalid the references to sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" in the Immigration Act; the government appealed in July 2024. The UNDP reports that Namibia's courts decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2024 and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested. The government told the UN it had no intention of repealing the colonial-era sodomy law, which has not been believed used since independence in 1990.

Gender-marker changes are available under section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and described as "not problematic" by the Legal Assistance Centre (2015). Article 10 of the Constitution omits gender identity and sexual orientation, though "other status" should encompass them per the UN Human Rights Committee.

Residence rights at the border have been contested for decades: in 2001 a Namibian woman's German wife Elisabeth Frank won a Supreme Court permanent residence permit without the court endorsing same-sex relationships, and in January 2018 Daniel Digashu won a court petition to enter Namibia while his case was reviewed.

Public displays of affection between two men can still be treated as "immoral" behaviour punishable under the Combating of Immoral Practices Act of 1980. Organised political hostility exists: a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters launched in 2014 with identical branding but an explicitly anti-gay stance, and the SWAPO Party Youth League is listed among parties opposing LGBTQ rights.

The Namibia's Broadcasting Code for Broadcasting Licensees 2018 (General Notice No. 602) bars licensees from broadcasting material advocating hatred based on gender or sexual orientation, sanctions violence or unlawful conduct on those grounds, and prohibits material likely to incite hatred or severe ridicule against persons because of sexual orientation where that constitutes incitement to harm.

Open expression has grown without government impediment: OutRight Namibia organised Namibia's first pride parades, with the Windhoek march of December 2013 drawing about 100 people, around 200 marching in June 2017, and hundreds marching in Windhoek and Swakopmund in December 2018. The first Namibian Lesbian Festival was held in Windhoek in November 2017 with more than sixty young lesbians from eight regions, repeated in November 2018.

Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May 2018 at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West, offering HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab called it "a first."

Health professionals are bound by the Ethical Guidelines for Health Professionals (2010, Health Professions Councils of Namibia), whose Sections 2.1.5, 2.6 and 3.2.2 require that personal beliefs not prejudice patient care and bar discrimination including on sexual orientation. The Ministry of Health and Social Services' Patient Charter makes "Impartiality" a core value requiring equal treatment irrespective of sex, gender and sexuality. However, the 2009 Ministry regulations on scope of practice for clinical and educational psychologists still treat "sexual and gender identity" as disorders.

Blood donor screening is relationship-based rather than orientation-based: no more than one sexual partner in the past six months regardless of sexual orientation or gender, with people suspected of an STI such as HIV or syphilis barred.

The Southern Africa Litigation Centre documented constitutional and administrative barriers facing trans Namibians in its 2017 analysis. The Namibian Gays and Lesbian Movement organises educational programs, and MPower Community Trust provides sexual health awareness for gay and bisexual men. The 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommended SOGI non-discrimination legislation.
tangentialFactors:
Namibia's enforcement gap between court rulings and administrative practice mirrors a broader regional pattern documented in the UNDP report 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' (December 2024), which notes that implementation of pro-equality judgments across the continent remains contested.

Organised political hostility to LGBT rights in Namibia includes a local replica of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters launched in 2014 with explicitly anti-gay messaging, and the SWAPO Party Youth League's opposition. Parliament's late-2024 act forbidding recognition of same-sex marriages performed abroad represents an institutional counter-current to the Supreme Court's May 2023 ruling.

The 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation have not produced corresponding statutory reform. The government's stated position to the UN that it has no intention of repealing the sodomy law signals continued official resistance despite the June 2024 High Court ruling invalidating related Immigration Act provisions.

outOfScopeNotes:

The government's appeal of the 21 June 2024 High Court ruling invalidating sodomy and "unnatural sexual offences" references in the Immigration Act was filed in July 2024; the outcome of that appeal is not sourced.

Whether the Supreme Court's gender-recognition orders have since been applied beyond named applicants, and whether immigration practice toward Daniel Digashu has changed after the December 2024 act, are not sourced.

Current enforcement of the Combating of Immoral Practices Act 1980 against public displays of affection between men, and any recent prosecutions under it, are not documented in the inventory.

The status of the 2009 Ministry regulations classifying "sexual and gender identity" as disorders, and whether they have been amended or repealed, is unresolved in the sourced material.
